question: ViT says it follows the original Transformer 'as closely as possible'. Which parts of the Transformer encoder does ViT keep, and how does its encoder differ from the one in 'Attention Is All You Need' (input handling, position information, normalisation placement, feed-forward activation)?
reference_answer: ViT keeps the Transformer encoder structure of alternating multi-head self-attention and position-wise MLP/feed-forward blocks with residual connections and layer normalisation, and uses the encoder only. Differences: (1) input - ViT splits an image into patches, linearly projects them and prepends a learnable [class] token, whereas the Transformer embeds discrete input tokens; (2) position information - ViT uses standard learnable 1D position embeddings, the Transformer uses fixed sinusoidal encodings (though it found learned embeddings nearly identical); (3) normalisation - the Transformer computes LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) after the residual addition, while ViT applies layer norm before every block and residual connections after every block; (4) the feed-forward layer uses ReLU in the Transformer and GELU in ViT. The Transformer paper additionally has a decoder with encoder-decoder attention.

## What ViT keeps from the original Transformer encoder

ViT states explicitly that "In model design we follow the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as closely as possible" [ViT, p.3], and specifically:

- **Overall encoder structure**: "The Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al., 2017) consists of alternating layers of multiheaded self-attention (MSA, see Appendix A) and MLP blocks" [ViT, p.3].
- **Multi-head self-attention mechanism itself**: ViT's Appendix A defines standard qkv self-attention and multi-head attention (MSA) with query/key/value projections, softmax(qkᵗ/√D_h)v, and concatenation of heads followed by a projection [ViT, p.13] — the same formulation as in the original Transformer's scaled dot-product and multi-head attention (Eq. 1, "MultiHead(Q,K,V) = Concat(head1,...,headh)Wᴼ") [Transformer, p.4-5].
- **Residual connections**: "residual connections after every block" [ViT, p.3], matching the original Transformer's residual-connection-around-each-sublayer design [Transformer, p.3].
- **Two-layer feed-forward (MLP) block per layer**, analogous to the original's position-wise feed-forward network with two linear transformations [Transformer, p.5] — ViT: "The MLP contains two layers" [ViT, p.4].

## How ViT's encoder differs

**1. Input handling.** The original Transformer encoder takes a 1D sequence of token embeddings for text [Transformer, p.2-3]. ViT instead reshapes an image into flattened 2D patches xp ∈ ℝ^(N×(P²·C)) and maps them to D dimensions via a trainable linear projection (Eq. 1), then prepends a learnable "[class]" token (borrowed from BERT, not from the original Transformer) whose final-layer output serves as the image representation [ViT, p.3]: "Similar to BERT's [class] token, we prepend a learnable embedding to the sequence of embedded patches... whose state at the output of the Transformer encoder... serves as the image representation."

**2. Position information.** ViT uses "standard learnable 1D position embeddings," stating they "have not observed significant performance gains from using more advanced 2D-aware position embeddings" [ViT, p.3], and these are added to patch embeddings (Eq. 1) [ViT, p.4]. The original Transformer's default is fixed sinusoidal positional encodings: "PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/dmodel))... PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(...)" chosen so the model "may... extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training" [Transformer, p.6]. The original paper notes it also tried learned positional embeddings and got "nearly identical results" [Transformer, p.6], but its main/default scheme is sinusoidal, whereas ViT's default is learned.

**3. Normalization placement.** ViT applies LayerNorm (LN) *before* each sub-block (pre-norm), per Eq. 2–3: "z′ℓ = MSA(LN(zℓ−1)) + zℓ−1" and "zℓ = MLP(LN(z′ℓ)) + z′ℓ," explicitly stating "Layernorm (LN) is applied before every block, and residual connections after every block (Wang et al., 2019; Baevski & Auli, 2019)" [ViT, p.3]. The original Transformer applies LayerNorm *after* each sub-layer, combined with the residual: "the output of each sub-layer is LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))" [Transformer, p.3] — i.e., post-norm rather than pre-norm.

**4. Feed-forward activation.** ViT's MLP uses a GELU nonlinearity: "The MLP contains two layers with a GELU non-linearity" [ViT, p.4]. The original Transformer's feed-forward network uses ReLU: "FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2" [Transformer, p.5].

**Additional structural difference (not explicitly asked but evident):** ViT uses only an encoder — there is no decoder stack, no encoder-decoder cross-attention, and no causal masking of self-attention, since the self-attention layers in ViT are applied globally over all patch tokens for classification [ViT, p.3-4], unlike the original Transformer's encoder-decoder architecture where the decoder's self-attention is masked to preserve autoregressive generation [Transformer, p.3].

## What ViT keeps from the original Transformer

ViT states explicitly: "In model design we follow the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) as closely as possible... The Transformer encoder (Vaswani et al., 2017) consists of alternating layers of multiheaded self-attention (MSA, see Appendix A) and MLP blocks (Eq. 2, 3)" [ViT, p.3]. The appendix confirms the attention mechanism itself is unchanged: "Standard qkv self-attention (SA, Vaswani et al. (2017)) is a popular building block... Multihead self-attention (MSA) is an extension of SA in which we run k self-attention operations... in parallel, and project their concatenated outputs" [ViT, p.13] — this matches the scaled dot-product / multi-head attention formulation in "Attention Is All You Need" [Transformer, p.4-5]. ViT also keeps the basic pattern of a residual connection around each sub-layer [ViT, p.3], and a position-wise feed-forward (MLP) block applied after the attention block, paralleling the Transformer's "position-wise fully connected feed-forward network" [Transformer, p.3].

## Where ViT's encoder differs

**1. Input handling.**
- Transformer: encoder input is a sequence of word/subword token embeddings fed directly into the stack [Transformer, p.2-3].
- ViT: the image is reshaped into flattened 2D patches, linearly projected to a constant dimension D via a trainable linear projection, and a learnable "[class]" token (`xclass`) is prepended to the sequence, whose output representation is later used for classification: "we prepend a learnable embedding to the sequence of embedded patches (z0_0 = xclass), whose state at the output of the Transformer encoder (z0_L) serves as the image representation" [ViT, p.3].

**2. Position information.**
- Transformer: uses fixed sinusoidal positional encodings, "sine and cosine functions of different frequencies," added to the input embeddings at the bottom of the encoder/decoder stacks, chosen partly because they "may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training" [Transformer, p.6]. (A learned-embedding variant was tested as an ablation and found "nearly identical" [Transformer, p.6].)
- ViT: uses "standard learnable 1D position embeddings," added to the patch embeddings, stating "we have not observed significant performance gains from using more advanced 2D-aware position embeddings" [ViT, p.3]. So ViT's default is the learned embedding that the original Transformer only used as a secondary comparison, not its primary (sinusoidal) choice.

**3. Normalization placement.**
- Transformer: post-norm — "the output of each sub-layer is LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))," i.e., the residual sum is computed first and LayerNorm applied afterward [Transformer, p.3].
- ViT: pre-norm — "Layernorm (LN) is applied before every block, and residual connections after every block (Wang et al., 2019; Baevski & Auli, 2019)," formalized as z′_ℓ = MSA(LN(z_{ℓ−1})) + z_{ℓ−1} and z_ℓ = MLP(LN(z′_ℓ)) + z′_ℓ [ViT, p.3-4]. So LN is applied to the input of each block rather than to the post-residual output.

**4. Feed-forward activation.**
- Transformer: the position-wise feed-forward network uses ReLU: FFN(x) = max(0, xW1+b1)W2+b2 [Transformer, p.5].
- ViT: "The MLP contains two layers with a GELU non-linearity" [ViT, p.3-4].

**Summary:** ViT reuses the Transformer's core computational block — alternating multi-head self-attention and a two-layer feed-forward/MLP sub-layer, each wrapped in a residual connection [ViT, p.3; Transformer, p.3] — but changes (a) the input (image patches + prepended class token instead of raw token embeddings, ViT p.3), (b) the positional information (learned 1D position embeddings vs. the Transformer's sinusoidal encodings, ViT p.3 vs. Transformer p.6), (c) normalization placement (pre-LN vs. the Transformer's post-LN, ViT p.3-4 vs. Transformer p.3), and (d) the activation in the feed-forward block (GELU vs. ReLU, ViT p.3-4 vs. Transformer p.5).

question: MAE and I-JEPA both mask parts of an image and use a ViT encoder on the visible part. What does each method predict and with what loss, and what evidence does the I-JEPA paper give that predicting in representation space matters?
reference_answer: MAE reconstructs the pixel values of the masked patches with a lightweight decoder (mean squared error computed only on masked patches); the encoder sees only visible patches and normalised pixels work slightly better (Table 1d, ViT-L/16: 85.4 vs 84.9 fine-tuning, 73.9 vs 73.5 linear probing). I-JEPA is non-generative: a predictor (narrow ViT) predicts the representations of target blocks from a context block, the targets come from a target encoder that is an exponential moving average of the context encoder, and the loss is average L2 distance in representation space. In I-JEPA's own ablation (Table 7, ViT-L/16, linear probe on 1% of ImageNet labels), using target-encoder outputs gave 66.9 top-1 versus 40.7 when the loss was in pixel space, and the authors say they 'conjecture' representation-space loss is a crucial component. I-JEPA also reports about 7% slower iterations than MAE but roughly 5x fewer iterations to converge. Caveat: the pixel-space variant is I-JEPA's own ablation (different epochs: 500 vs 800), not the MAE paper's setup, and MAE does not test representation-space targets.

candidates.answer:
## What each method predicts

**MAE** masks random patches (typically 75%) of the input image, encodes only the visible patches with a ViT encoder, and then uses a lightweight decoder (with mask tokens inserted) to **reconstruct the missing patches in pixel space**: "Our MAE reconstructs the input by predicting the pixel values for each masked patch... The decoder's output is reshaped to form a reconstructed image" [MAE, p.4]. The loss is **mean squared error (MSE) between reconstructed and original pixels, computed only on masked patches**: "Our loss function computes the mean squared error (MSE) between the reconstructed and original images in the pixel space. We compute the loss only on masked patches, similar to BERT" [MAE, p.4]. (A variant normalizes per-patch pixel values as the target, which slightly improves results [MAE, p.4].)

**I-JEPA** samples a context block and several target blocks from an image; the context is encoded by a ViT context-encoder, and the targets are obtained from the **output of a separate target-encoder** (an EMA copy of the context encoder), not from pixels. A predictor network takes the context encoder's output plus positional mask tokens and **predicts the target blocks' representations in embedding space**: "the predictor gϕ(·, ·) takes as input the output of the context encoder sx and a mask token... and outputs a patch-level prediction ŝy(i)" [I-JEPA, p.4]. The loss is the **average L2 distance between predicted and target patch-level representations**: "The loss is simply the average L2 distance between the predicted patch-level representations ŝy(i) and the target patch-level representation sy(i)" [I-JEPA, p.4].

## Evidence that predicting in representation space matters (I-JEPA)

The I-JEPA paper directly ablates this choice: "Table 7 compares low-shot performance on 1% ImageNet-1K using a linear probe when the loss is computed in pixel-space versus representation space... it is clear that predicting in pixel-space leads to a significant degradation in the linear probing performance" [I-JEPA, p.7].

The numbers (Table 7, ViT-L/16, ImageNet-1% linear eval):
- Target = Target-Encoder Output (representation space), 500 epochs → **66.9** top-1
- Target = Pixels, 800 epochs → **40.7** top-1

[I-JEPA, p.7]

That is a drop of 66.9 − 40.7 = **26.2 percentage points** when switching from representation-space targets to pixel-space targets — despite the pixel-space variant being trained for *more* epochs (800 vs. 500). The paper interprets this as showing that "a crucial component of I-JEPA is that the loss is computed entirely in representation space, thereby giving the target encoder the ability to produce abstract prediction targets, for which irrelevant pixel-level details are eliminated" [I-JEPA, p.7].

This ablation is the specific evidence the paper provides; it does not report additional controlled experiments (e.g., varying architecture/compute) isolating this factor beyond Table 7.

## Source of targets in each method

**Distillation:** The targets are the soft output probabilities (soft target distribution) produced by a large, already-trained "cumbersome model" — either a single large highly regularized model or an ensemble of models — run at a high softmax temperature. "In the simplest form of distillation, knowledge is transferred to the distilled model by training it on a transfer set and using a soft target distribution for each case in the transfer set that is produced by using the cumbersome model with a high temperature in its softmax" [Distillation, p.3, Abstract]. This cumbersome/teacher model is trained separately and beforehand (e.g., as an ensemble of 10 models trained on hard labels), and its outputs are then transferred to the smaller distilled model: "our distillation approach is able to extract more useful information from the training set than simply using the hard labels to train a single model... the improvement in WER achieved by the ensemble is transferred to the distilled model" [Distillation, p.5]. So here hard labels ARE used — but to train the teacher model first; the student is then trained primarily on the teacher's soft targets (optionally combined with hard labels, as temperature reverts to 1 at deployment and training uses the high-temperature soft targets) [Distillation, p.3, Abstract; p.5].

**BYOL:** The targets come from a **target network** that has the identical architecture to the online network but a different set of weights ξ, which are not learned by gradient descent but are an **exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network's own weights θ**: "its parameters ξ are an exponential moving average of the online parameters θ" [BYOL, p.3, section 3.1]. No separate pre-trained model and no labels are used to produce these targets — they are "bootstrapped" from the network's own evolving representation: "we propose to directly bootstrap the representations... BYOL trains its online network to predict the target network's representation of another augmented view of the same image" [BYOL, p.2, Abstract]. The whole training pipeline is label-free (self-supervised); BYOL is only evaluated afterward using labels in the linear-evaluation/semi-supervised protocols [BYOL, p.2, Abstract], but the target-generation process itself uses no labels.

## BYOL's comparison to Mean Teacher

BYOL explicitly identifies Mean Teacher (MT) as the closest existing approach using a slow-moving average target network, but highlights two key differences:

1. **Mean Teacher is semi-supervised and uses labels; BYOL does not.** "In the semi-supervised setting..., an unsupervised loss is combined with a classification loss over a handful of labels... mean teacher (MT) also uses a slow-moving average network, called teacher, to produce targets for an online network, called student. An ℓ2 consistency loss between the softmax predictions of the teacher and the student is added to the classification loss" [BYOL, p.3, section 2].

2. **Without the classification loss, the MT-style approach collapses, whereas BYOL does not — because of BYOL's added predictor.** "While [20] demonstrates the effectiveness of MT in the semi-supervised learning case, in Section 5 we show that a similar approach collapses when removing the classification loss. In contrast, BYOL introduces an additional predictor on top of the online network, which prevents collapse" [BYOL, p.3, section 2].

This is reiterated later: "Removing the predictor in BYOL results in an unsupervised version of MT with no classification loss that" [collapses, continuing the ablation discussion] [BYOL, p.9, section 5]. Also note a structural difference: MT's consistency loss is computed directly on softmax/logit outputs of student vs. teacher [BYOL, p.3, section 2], whereas BYOL's online network has an extra predictor stage (fθ → gθ → qθ) beyond what the target network computes (fξ → gξ only) [BYOL, p.3, section 3.1], and BYOL's loss operates on projected representations rather than classification logits.

**Summary:** Distillation's targets come from an externally, separately pre-trained (and possibly label-trained) cumbersome teacher model's soft softmax outputs at high temperature [Distillation, p.3, p.5]. BYOL's targets come from an EMA of the online network's own weights, requiring no separate teacher and no labels [BYOL, p.3, section 3.1; p.2, Abstract]. BYOL treats Mean Teacher as the closest prior slow-moving-average-target method, but notes MT requires a classification loss on labels and collapses without it, whereas BYOL avoids collapse via its predictor and remains fully unsupervised [BYOL, p.3, section 2].

# How targets are supplied in Distillation vs. BYOL

## Distillation (Hinton, Vinyals & Dean)

The targets come from a **separately, fully-trained "cumbersome model"** — either a large ensemble of models or a single large heavily-regularized model — trained *before* distillation begins:

- "The cumbersome model could be an ensemble of separately trained models or a single very large model trained with a very strong regularizer such as dropout" [Distillation, p.1].
- The target model is trained normally, typically with **hard labels**, to maximize average log probability of the correct class. The targets used for the small model are the **soft class probabilities** this trained model produces, obtained by raising the softmax temperature: "knowledge is transferred to the distilled model by training it on a transfer set and using a soft target distribution for each case in the transfer set that is produced by using the cumbersome model with a high temperature in its softmax" [Distillation, p.3].
- Labels are optionally reintroduced during the transfer step itself: "When the correct labels are known for all or some of the transfer set, this method can be significantly improved by also training the distilled model to produce the correct labels," via a weighted average of a soft-target cross-entropy loss and a hard-target cross-entropy loss [Distillation, p.3].
- In the ensemble case, the soft targets can be the "arithmetic or geometric mean" of the individual trained models' predictive distributions [Distillation, p.2].

So: targets = outputs of an **independently pre-trained** (label-supervised) model/ensemble, used post-hoc; the target model does not change during distillation.

## BYOL (Grill et al.)

The targets come from a **target network that is itself a continuously-updated exponential moving average (EMA) of the online network being trained** — not a separately pretrained model:

- "The target network provides the regression targets to train the online network, and its parameters ξ are an exponential moving average of the online parameters θ... ξ ← τξ + (1−τ)θ" [BYOL, p.3].
- No labels are used at all: BYOL is self-supervised — the online network predicts the target network's projection of a *different augmented view of the same (unlabeled) image* [BYOL, p.3–4]. Labels appear only later in optional linear-evaluation/semi-supervised fine-tuning, not in producing the targets.
- The target network co-evolves with the online network during training (it is not a fixed, finished model); only the online encoder is kept at the end [BYOL, p.3–4].

## BYOL's discussion of Mean Teacher (its closest comparison for the slow-moving-average target)

BYOL explicitly compares itself to **Mean Teacher (MT)**, the semi-supervised method it treats as closest to its own target-network mechanism:

- "Mean teacher (MT) [20] also uses a slow-moving average network, called teacher, to produce targets for an online network, called student. An ℓ2 consistency loss between the softmax predictions of the teacher and the student is added to the classification loss." [BYOL, p.3]
- Key difference: MT relies on **a classification loss over labels** to "ground the training" of its EMA target. BYOL shows that removing this classification loss (making MT's mechanism fully unsupervised) causes collapse: "[20] demonstrates the effectiveness of MT in the semi-supervised learning case, in Section 5 we show that a similar approach collapses when removing the classification loss. In contrast, BYOL introduces an additional predictor on top of the online network, which prevents collapse." [BYOL, p.3]
- This is confirmed quantitatively in the ablations: "Removing the predictor in BYOL results in an unsupervised version of MT with no classification loss that uses image augmentations instead of the original architectural noise (e.g., dropout). This variant of BYOL collapses (Row 7 of Table 5) which suggests that the additional predictor is critical to prevent collapse in an unsupervised scenario." [BYOL, p.9–10]

So BYOL's argument is: MT's slow-moving-average target works because labels anchor the student via a classification loss; take the labels away and MT's approach collapses, whereas BYOL avoids collapse without labels by adding a **predictor** on the online branch — this predictor (plus the EMA target) is what BYOL identifies as the key ingredient MT lacks.
